The treaty was ratified, the amendment assented to, and it was proclaimed Dec. 5, 1861. Federal officials did admit in 1863 that many bands were not part of it and still claimed their country.

source_title: Act of June 30, 1834, secs. 1, 10, 11; Bates v. Clark (1877)
source_quote: Congress has not thought it necessary to make any new definition of Indian country.
corrected_summary: The 1834 Act defined Indian country, let agents remove intruders, and fined anyone settling on land "belonging, secured, or granted by treaty" to a tribe $1,000. It did not declare Cheyenne title as such, and it did not bar all non-traders: it licensed traders and required passports of foreigners. The federal government did not remove the gold-rush settlers. The Act was not "rescinded in 1873": in 1877 the Supreme Court (Bates v. Clark) still applied its definition of Indian country. Linking non-enforcement to Sand Creek is TREC's argument.
notes: Sec. 11 penalty applies to land secured by treaty; before 1851 no treaty secured Cheyenne land, so sec. 11 arguably applied only after Fort Laramie 1851. "39 years" and "rescinded 1873" are uncited; the Revised Statutes (1874) carried most sections forward.

source_title: TREC pp. 240-241, quoting Jefferson Davis via a secondary work
source_quote: In every treaty we evaluated, the process was the same. Treaty commissioners represented the United States government; most often, these
notes: Author generalization; record as TREC's characterization. Counter-example in the record: the Senate journal shows the 1851 text was changed only by the Senate, not the commissioners; but at Medicine Lodge and elsewhere commissioners did alter drafts. "Chicago Re-write" is Lakota oral tradition reported by TREC.

source_title: Sheldon Spotted Elk (2012 law review article) as quoted by TREC pp. 241-244

notes: Governance description is Spotted Elk's (scholarly, via TREC). Using it as the yardstick for valid signatures is TREC's interpretive frame; attribute it. Primary support that chiefs themselves invoked whole-nation consent: Gerry 1863 (ARCIA 1863 p. 130) "they would not make any treaty to cede any of their lands until the whole nation north and south were called together".

source_title: Treaty with the Cheyenne Tribe, July 6, 1825
source_quote: Ta-ton-ca-pa, or the buffaloe head
corrected_summary: First Cheyenne treaty, July 6, 1825, at the mouth of the Teton River: a trade-and-friendship treaty with no land cession. The Cheyenne agreed to give safe conduct to persons authorized by the United States and not to molest Americans travelling to and from New Mexico; it did not open their country to emigrants generally. The signers' names are written in Lakota form (e.g. Ta-ton-ca, Shong-ge-mon-e-to, Oh-kee-che-ta). The Council of 44 approval is TREC's account.
corrected_instrument_cite: Treaty of July 6, 1825, 7 Stat. 255; Kappler II 232 (1904 ed.; p. 164 in the 1903 ed.)
notes: Art. 4 text in Kappler (local file /tmp/claude-0/-home-user/d66bb275-6adb-522a-9fbd-8e5b55892ae3/scratchpad/psl/library/kappler/kappler-vol2-treaties.txt): "give safe conduct to all persons who may be legally authorized by the United States to pass through their country". Lakota reading of names is my linguistic reading (tatanka, sunkmanitu, akicita), consistent with TREC.

source_title: D.D. Mitchell to Commissioner, Nov. 11, 1851, in Kappler IV
source_quote: the settling up of all former complaints on the part of the Indians for the destruction of their buffalo, timber, grass, etc., caused by the passage of the whites through their country
corrected_summary: Emigrant traffic on the Platte road damaged buffalo, timber and grass, and the 1851 commissioner himself named settling those complaints as a purpose of the treaty. TREC's dating (from about 1845, sharply after 1849) and the word "illegal" for emigrants are TREC's.
notes: Emigrants crossing on the trail were not plainly illegal under the 1834 Act (no passport needed for citizens); settlers were. Keep "illegal immigrants" as TREC wording.

source_title: Missouri Republican dispatches (A.B. Chambers, B. Gratz Brown), 1851, as quoted by TREC p. 246 via a secondary work
source_quote: We do not want your land, horses, robes, nor anything you have; but we come to advise with you
corrected_instrument_cite: Treaty of Fort Laramie, Sept. 17, 1851, Kappler II 594 (1904 ed.); 11 Stat. 749 (stub only); full text Kappler IV 1065
notes: Speech is from newspaper reports, not the treaty file. The 50-year promise is confirmed by Mitchell's own transmittal: "the promised annuity of $50,000 for 50 years" (Kappler IV 1072). To settle the speech wording, check the Missouri Republican, Oct-Nov 1851 (reprinted in Hafen and Young, Fort Laramie, 1938).

source_title: Treaty of Fort Laramie 1851, Art. 6, as printed in Kappler IV
source_quote: having selected principals or head chiefs for their respective nations, through whom all national business will hereafter be conducted, do hereby bind themselves to sustain said chiefs and their successors during good behavior
corrected_summary: Article 6 has the nations "having selected" head chiefs and binding themselves to sustain them; the text says the nations selected them, though TREC and historians say the commissioners pushed it. That this subverted Council of 44 governance and set a precedent for collective responsibility is TREC's interpretation.
notes: Medicine Chief error claim is TREC's. Who chose the head chiefs needs the council record (Missouri Republican).

source_title: Treaty of Fort Laramie 1851 signature list and 1853 Cheyenne-Arapaho assent, in Kappler IV
source_quote: Cheyennes: Wah-ha-nis-satta (his x mark); Voist-ti-toe-vetz (his x mark); Nahk-ko-me-ien (his x mark); Koh-kah-y-wh-cum-est (his x mark).
corrected_summary: Four Cheyenne marks are on the 1851 treaty. The assent to the Senate amendment translates them as The Man that Walks Out, White Cow, Old Bark and White Antelope. TREC's list (Stone Forehead, Whiteface Bull, White Antelope, Bear Feather) matches only on White Antelope by name. The band identifications and the claim that no Northern chief signed are TREC's and not shown by the treaty.
notes: TREC itself hedges ("may have signed"). The signature list fixes the count at four Cheyenne and three Arapaho, which also resolves the four-versus-six inconsistency noted in round 1.

source_title: Treaty of Fort Laramie 1851, Art. 5
source_quote: The territory of the Cheyennes and Arrapahoes, commencing at the Red Bute, or the place where the road leaves the north fork of the Platte River; thence up the north fork of the Platte River to its source
notes: Article 5 assigns one joint territory to "the Cheyennes and Arrapahoes" with no internal line, and reserves "rights or claims they may have to other lands" and hunting, fishing and passage. That joint assignment "violated sovereignty" is TREC's view. ICC Docket 329 treated this as recognized title.

source_title: Treaty of Fort Laramie 1851, Art. 5; Agreement of 1876 ratified Feb. 28, 1877, Art. 1
source_quote: relinquish and cede to the United States all the territory lying outside
corrected_summary: Article 5 did keep the privilege of hunting, fishing and passing over the described tracts. Whether those privileges survive is TREC's argument. Later instruments signed by Northern Cheyenne and Northern Arapaho leaders reached them: the May 10, 1868 treaty kept only a right to roam and hunt while game lasted, and the 1876 agreement (ratified 1877) ceded all territory outside the Sioux reservation "including all privileges of hunting".
notes: Not a settled survival of rights; present as TREC's legal argument against later relinquishments whose legitimacy the Northern nations contest.

source_title: Treaty of Fort Laramie 1851, Arts. 3-4; Act of June 30, 1834, sec. 11
source_quote: whilst lawfully residing in or passing through their respective territories
corrected_summary: Article 3 bound the US to protect the nations against depredations by US citizens but named no enforcement method; the 1834 Act's settler penalty was $1,000 (sec. 11) and removal (sec. 10), and was not used against the gold-rush settlers. TREC's claim that "lawfully residing" conflicts with the 1834 Act is overstated: licensed traders, agents and their employees could lawfully reside in Indian country.
notes: $500 penalties in the 1834 Act apply to other offenses (e.g. trading without license, hunting), not settlement.

source_title: Treaty of Fort Laramie 1851, Art. 8; Upper Platte agent Loree certificate, Aug. 19, 1863
source_quote: not to deliver their annuity goods to them until after the time appointed for the council
notes: Art. 8 text confirmed: the US "may withhold the whole or a portion of the annuities... from the nation so offending". Annuity leverage in practice: the 1853 appropriation conditioned payment on assent to the Senate amendment (10 Stat. 238, quoted Kappler IV 1071), and in 1863 Agent Loree held back annuity goods to obtain an agreement to abide by Fort Wise. "Collective punishment" is TREC's term.

source_title: Kappler IV (1929), Treaty of Fort Laramie 1851 footnote, Indian Office memorandum, Senate Journal extract, and tribal assents
source_quote: Assent of all tribes was procured, the last acceptance being by the Crows September 18, 1854.
corrected_summary: The Senate ratified the treaty on May 24, 1852 (not Sept. 17, 1851), cutting the annuity from 50 years to 10 plus up to 5 at the President's discretion, subject to tribal acceptance. Kappler's 1929 volume prints written assents from all eight nations, 1853-1854, including six Cheyenne marks (the four original signers plus Little Chief and Black Leg) and Arapaho marks including all three original signers. The treaty was never proclaimed because the Interior Department failed to certify the assents to State, and its text was left out of the Statutes at Large. TREC's claims that only three nations assented, that Kappler admitted in 1929 the tribes did not agree, and that fewer original signers appear on the assent are contradicted.
corrected_instrument_cite: Kappler II 594 (1904); Kappler IV 1065-1081 (1929); 11 Stat. 749 (stub note)
notes: Fillmore did not "refuse to sign": the President asked whether the amendment could be adopted without resubmission and Commissioner Lea said no (May 29, 1852). The "never got together" endorsement was not found in Kappler IV; it may be on one file copy (Prucha). The unilateral cut itself is confirmed. Unilateral Senate change with after-the-fact assent obtained while annuities were conditioned on it (10 Stat. 238 proviso) is the defensible framing.

source_title: Commissioner Luke Lea to Secretary A.H.H. Stuart, May 29, 1852
source_quote: how such a proceeding, in view of the legal principles involved, can be considered anything but a mockery of the highest and most solemn form of contract it is difficult to perceive.
notes: Lea's point was that the amendment must go back to the tribes; the government then did obtain assents (1853-54). The same letter calls the Indians "wild and savage" and urges prompt appropriations, so quote in context.

source_title: Roy v. United States, 45 Ct. Cl. 177 (1910), and Moore v. United States, 32 Ct. Cl. 593 (1897), as quoted in Kappler IV; New York Indians v. United States, 170 U.S. 1 (1898)
source_quote: These Indians were our wards, and we thus occupied a fiduciary relation to them.
corrected_instrument_cite: Roy v. United States, 45 Ct. Cl. 177 (1910); Moore v. United States, 32 Ct. Cl. 593 (1897); New York Indians v. United States, 170 U.S. 1, 23 (1898)

"170 U.S. 23" is a pin cite within 170 U.S. 1 (decided April 11, 1898), and the case did hold an unpublished Senate proviso inoperative. Kellogg refusal (1920s) not checked; Frank B. Kellogg was Secretary of State 1925-29.

source_title: Kappler IV footnote; ICC Dockets 329 and 348, Order of Dec. 6, 1961
source_cite: Kappler IV 1065 n.1; 10 Ind. Cl. Comm. 1, 108 (1961)
source_quote: There is no doubt that the Fort Laramie treaty is in full force and effect.
corrected_summary: TREC says the ICC erred by using an "unratified" 1851 treaty. The treaty was ratified with amendment by the Senate (May 24, 1852), assented to by all tribes by 1854, and held binding by the Court of Claims; it was never proclaimed. The ICC treated Article 5 as recognition of Cheyenne-Arapaho title, based on facts the government stipulated.
notes: Whether recognition by the 1851 treaty was the right basis for valuation is a fair legal question; "never ratified" is not.

source_title: Missouri Republican (A.B. Chambers / B. Gratz Brown) dispatch, 1851, as quoted by TREC pp. 253-256
source_quote: They are so numerous and so well banded together that the chiefs can do nothing with them.
notes: Newspaper account via a secondary; TREC calls it "unreported" but it is from the published dispatches. Check Missouri Republican, Oct. 1851 (or Hafen and Young 1938). Quote is a white reporter's view.

source_title: Kansas-Nebraska Act, May 30, 1854, secs. 1, 19, 37
source_quote: construed to impair the rights of person or property now pertaining to
corrected_summary: The Act put present-day eastern Colorado into Kansas Territory (south of 40 degrees N) and Nebraska Territory (north of it), while saying Indian rights were not impaired until extinguished by treaty and that treaties must be "faithfully and rigidly observed". It excluded from the territories only lands whose treaty said they could not be included without tribal consent; the Cheyenne-Arapaho lands had no such clause, so they were inside the territories.
notes: Correct TREC: Kansas Territory alone did not take the "entire" Front Range; the Boulder-Fort Collins area was in Nebraska Territory.

source_title: Treaty of Fort Laramie 1851 signature list, Kappler IV
source_quote: Sioux: Mah-toe-wha-you-whey (his x mark)
corrected_summary: Grattan's detachment fired on a Brule camp near Fort Laramie in August 1854 and was destroyed; Conquering Bear (Mato Wayuhi, first Sioux signer of the 1851 treaty) was killed. That he was "coerced" into signing is TREC's claim. The army attack killing ten Cheyenne and the 18 whites killed are TREC figures needing a source (likely the 1856 Platte Bridge and Fort Kearny clashes).
notes: Signature identification of Mah-toe-wha-you-whey as Conquering Bear is standard (Hafen); not stated in Kappler. Check ARCIA 1856 (Twiss report) for the 1856 Cheyenne casualties.

source_quote: The order from the War Department was issued on October 24th, 1856, eight days following the successful conclusion of the peace council with Thomas S. Twiss
notes: TREC gives two dates (Oct. 24, 1856 via Chalfant; April 10, 1857 under Floyd). Settle with Secretary of War annual report 1857 (Sen. Ex. Doc. 11, 35th Cong. 1st sess.) and ARCIA 1856 Twiss report. Sumner's 1857 campaign (Solomon's Fork, July 29, 1857) is well documented; "settled and forgiven by treaty" is Chalfant's characterization.

source_title: TREC p. 259 (secondary narrative, likely Powell or Hoig)
source_quote: The Southern leaders were agreeable to a new treaty as long as they could keep their lands
notes: Needs ARCIA 1857-1858 (Upper Arkansas agent Robert Miller / William Bent reports). Consistent with later primary statements (Gerry 1863) that chiefs would not cede land without the whole nation.

source_title: Agent S.G. Colley to Gov. Evans, Fort Lyon, Aug. 22, 1863
source_quote: I am more convinced than ever that they are one and the same Indians.
notes: The Upper Platte agency (Loree) and Upper Arkansas agency (Colley) were separate. Colley, writing of the "northern Arapahoes" at Fort Lyon, says they are the same people, supporting TREC's point that the North-South split was an administrative notion. Southern refusal of a separate peace is TREC's account.

source_title: Elbridge Gerry to Gov. Evans, Sept. 22, 1863, in ARCIA 1863
source_quote: they would not make any treaty to cede any of their lands until the whole nation north and south were called together to see and hear for themselves
corrected_summary: TREC states (via Coel) that in 1860 the Council of 44 refused to attend Greenwood's council or give up land, and that Greenwood said he would make the treaty "over the heads of the Cheyenne". The 1860 events and the Greenwood quote rest on Coel (scholarly) and were not checked in the 1860 Commissioner's report. A primary source shows the same position in 1863: Cheyenne chiefs told Gerry they would cede no land until the whole nation, north and south, was called together.
notes: Royce 477 is only the 1861 reserve (ceded 1865). The Fort Wise cession of the 1851 territory is Royce 426 (Royce p. 824: "Cede all land claimed by them except one reserved tract"). Greenwood 1860 report: ARCIA 1860 (Greenwood to Thompson, Oct. 1860) needed; local uw-greenwood-1860 file is empty.

source_title: Treaty of Fort Wise signature list; Gerry report Sept. 22, 1863
source_quote: White Antelope told me that he never signed the treaty, and they all said that Block Kettle, who was in the village but not present, denied having signed it.
corrected_summary: Ten chiefs signed on Feb. 18, 1861: Arapaho Little Raven, Storm, Shave-Head, Big Mouth; Cheyenne Black Kettle, White Antelope, Lean Bear, Little Wolf, Tall Bear, and Left Hand or Namos (listed as Cheyenne). In 1863 White Antelope told trader Elbridge Gerry he never signed, and the chiefs said Black Kettle denied signing (Gerry's secondhand report, in the Commissioner's annual report). That they lacked Council of 44 authority and that Boone "randomly appointed" signers are TREC's claims via George Bent and Hyde.
notes: The same Gerry report says the chiefs called Fort Wise "a swindle; that they who signed it did not understand it." The treaty recites the signers were "duly authorized" by the tribes; that recital is the government's.

source_title: Treaty of Fort Laramie 1851 witness list; Treaty of Fort Wise witness list
source_quote: JOHN S. SMITH, U. S. Interpreter.
notes: At Fort Laramie 1851 John S. Smith was listed as "interpreter for Cheyennes" and John Pizelle (Poisal) as interpreter for the Arapahoes (Kappler IV 1067). At Fort Wise only John S. Smith and Robert Bent are listed, as "U. S. Interpreter". Whether Smith spoke Arapaho is not shown; TREC's claim is uncited (n.40). TREC's view that this "should legally invalidate" the treaty is its own.

source_title: Treaty of Fort Wise preamble
source_quote: representing the confederated tribes of Arapahoe and Cheyenne Indians of the Upper Arkansas River
notes: The phrase is in the treaty. TREC's claim that no confederation was ever agreed is plausible but is its own; the Civil War motive is speculation. The phrase also appears in the 1861 assent and Senate resolution.

source_title: Treaty of Fort Wise Art. 6; Loree agreement Aug. 19, 1863; ICC Order Dec. 6, 1961
source_cite: 12 Stat. 1165; ARCIA 1863 pp. 131-132; 10 Ind. Cl. Comm. 108
source_quote: agree that we will abide by any treaty that has been or may be made by our people with the United States
corrected_summary: Article 6 invited absent bands to join within a year or lose the treaty's benefits; its text does not suspend the cession (the "abeyance" reading is Coel's). It is not true that only one signature was ever obtained: on Aug. 19, 1863 five Upper Platte leaders (Arapaho Black Bear, Roman Nose, Friday; Cheyenne Spotted Horse, Shield) signed an agreement to abide by Fort Wise, given in exchange for their annuities and never sent to the Senate. The ICC held that the United States acquired the Northern half-interest by the May 10, 1868 treaty. "Never ceded north of the South Platte" is the Northern nations' and TREC's position, not the legal record.
notes: Gov. Evans himself wrote the 1863 paper "though not in proper treaty form, secures in effect an assent" and that a new agreement would give "an undoubted cession", showing officials saw the 1861 cession as doubtful for the Northern bands (ARCIA 1863 p. 125). Map as "contested cession".

source_title: Commissioner W.P. Dole, Annual Report 1863; TREC quoting 1862 report via ICC
source_quote: numbers of the bands were not included in the negotiations attending the treaty concluded with them at Fort Wise, whence arises the claim they so persistently urge that their right to roam at will throughout a country
corrected_summary: Federal officials did admit that some bands were not party to Fort Wise and still claimed the country. The Commissioner's 1863 report says many bands were not included and claim their right "has never been relinquished". The exact 1862 wording TREC quotes ("imperfect and indefinite... unperfected portion") was not seen in a primary copy.
notes: To settle the 1862 quote: ARCIA 1862 (H. Exec. Doc. 1, 37th Cong., 3d sess.), Colorado Superintendency; or ICC 10 Ind. Cl. Comm. 1 at 35-36 (local OCR too poor to search).

source_quote: Treaty of May LO, 1868 (15 S t a t . 655) t h e United S t a t e s a c q u i r e d t h e un-
corrected_summary: The ICC did not merely "suggest" it: it concluded as a matter of law that the United States acquired the Northern half-interest in the 1851 lands by the May 10, 1868 treaty, and found the consideration paid unconscionable. Article 2 of that treaty plainly relinquishes "all territory outside" the two named reservations, though it does not name Fort Wise. TREC's "ambiguous" is its own view.
notes: Quote is the raw OCR line (OCR reads "LO" for 10 and spaces letters); it continues "divided half interest of the Northern Cheyenne and Arapaho Indians". Verify against the PDF. 1865 commissioners statement to Southern bands not checked (Little Arkansas journal, ARCIA 1865).

The State Department letter TREC quotes (p. 268) says the amendment "has been assented to", which reads as written after the assent, not before the tribes met. source_quote: Sandy Fork of the Arkansas River and extending westwardly along the said river to the mouth of Purgatory River
corrected_summary: The reserve ran along the Arkansas from Sand Creek to the Purgatoire and south to New Mexico. The 53 million acre figure is TREC's and uncited; the ICC measured the 1851 Cheyenne-Arapaho territory at about 51.2 million acres. The overlap with a 25-mile military reserve and the "no-water land" name are TREC's, not in the treaty.

notes: Date is May 28, 1864 (TREC p. 194 says May 24). Smiley (1901) quote is secondary. "Never compensated / should be voided" is TREC's position; the ICC later paid for the 1851 lands as of 1865 values.

source_title: Pacific Railroad Act, July 1, 1862, secs. 1-3
source_quote: to the amount of five alternate sections per mile on each side of said railroad
corrected_summary: The 1862 Pacific Railroad Act granted a right of way 200 feet wide on each side of the track and five alternate sections per mile on each side (6,400 acres per mile), and directed the US to extinguish Indian title on those lands. John Evans of Colorado was named in the Act as one of the commissioners (corporators). That the 1862 Acts moved "stolen" land into the public domain is TREC's characterization.
corrected_instrument_cite: 12 Stat. 489; Homestead Act 12 Stat. 392; Morrill Act 12 Stat. 503
notes: TREC's "200-foot right-of-way" understates (200 ft each side). The 1864 amendment (13 Stat. 356) doubled the grant to ten sections per side.

source_title: Gov. Evans report 1863 and Commissioner Dole report 1863; Unrau, Prelude to War (1964)
source_quote: Arkansas river, and an undoubted cession of their claims to all other parts of
corrected_summary: U.S. Attorney S.E. Browne's 1863 opinion that land north and west of the South Platte had not been ceded is reported by Unrau (scholarly); the letter itself was not seen. Primary federal reports from 1863 show officials treated Northern-band assent as still needed: Evans sought a new agreement to secure "an undoubted cession". "Never ceded" is not the legal outcome; the ICC held the Northern interest passed by the 1868 treaty.
notes: Dole to Evans quote not checked (NARA RG 75, Colorado Superintendency, 1863). Browne to Usher, March 16, 1863 needed for the primary text.

source_title: Acting Commissioner Charles E. Mix to Gov. Evans, June 23, 1864; Evans annual report 1864
source_quote: It is not contemplated that the Indians should be collected and fed on the reservations, but they should be concentrated, if anywhere, about the buffalo range.
corrected_summary: The Mix letter (June 23, 1864) told Evans to keep the peace, not to feed Indians on the reservation, and to concentrate them about the buffalo range, and to contract no debts. It did not reject separating friendly from hostile Indians: Evans reports the department approved collecting the friendly Indians at places of safety. Evans ignoring Dole's 1863 council order is TREC's claim.
notes: Evans quotes the department telegram: "Act according to your best judgment with regard to friendly Indians, but do not exceed the appropriations" (ARCIA 1864 p. 218).

source_title: Gov. John Evans, proclamations of June 27 and Aug. 11, 1864, in ARCIA 1864; JCCW 1865
source_cite: ARCIA 1864 pp. 218-219, 230-231; JCCW 1865 Massacre of Cheyenne Indians p. IV
source_quote: authorizing all citizens of Colorado, either individually or in such parties as they may organize, to go in pursuit of all hostile Indians on the plains
corrected_summary: Evans's June 27, 1864 proclamation told friendly Indians to go to four places of safety (Fort Lyon for the Arkansas Cheyenne and Arapaho, Fort Larned, Fort Laramie, Camp Collins). His Aug. 11 proclamation authorized citizens to "kill and destroy" hostile Indians and to "hold to their own private use and benefit" property they captured. The Joint Committee on the Conduct of the War said this appealed to settlers' "cupidity". That it "led directly" to Sand Creek is TREC's argument; Sand Creek was carried out by U.S. volunteer troops under Chivington.
notes: The reward wording in TREC is a paraphrase; use the original words. "Declared war on all not at Fort Lyon" overstates the June 27 text.

source_quote: he surprised and murdered, in cold blood, the unsuspecting men, women, and children on Sand creek, who had every reason to believe they were under the protection of the United States
corrected_summary: The Joint Committee found that Chivington "surprised and murdered, in cold blood" people who had every reason to believe they were under U.S. protection, and found Evans's testimony marked by "prevarication and shuffling". It called for removing from office "those who have thus disgraced the government", without naming Evans. That Evans bore more responsibility than anyone is TREC's view.
notes: Military commission testimony: Sen. Ex. Doc. 26, 39th Cong. 2d sess. (local /tmp/claude-0/-home-user/d66bb275-6adb-522a-9fbd-8e5b55892ae3/scratchpad/psl/library/reports/SenExDoc26-39-2-SandCreek-GR_4292.txt). Chivington non-prosecution: he had left the service in Jan. 1865 (secondary).

source_quote: they put a lot of strychnine in a barrel of whisky and stuck it up where the Indians could get it ; that the Indians never touched it
corrected_summary: Ware reports a soldier's secondhand story that men at Gillette's Ranch put strychnine in a barrel of whisky for Indians to find, and that the Indians never touched it; Ware emptied the barrel. It is evidence of attempted poisoning, not of deaths. Tall Bull family and other oral accounts of poisoning are TREC's sources.
notes: Do not cite Ware as a poisoning death.

source_title: Indian Peace Commission resolutions, Chicago, Oct. 9, 1868

corrected_summary: The Peace Commission's Oct. 9, 1868 resolutions urged that tribes no longer be recognized as "domestic dependent nations", that the Indian Bureau move to the War Department, that Medicine Lodge roaming rights be abrogated, and that military force compel removal to reservations. Calling the Commission a pretense is TREC's view. The Sherman and Grant statements (New York Times, Oct. 16, 1868) and the Denver "Exterminate them!" story were not checked.
notes: Sheridan "only good Indian" attribution is disputed and uncited; do not map.

source_cite: Official Records, Ser. I, vol. 48, pt. 2, p. 1049 (also to Lt. Col. Walker, July 28, 1865, p. 1131)
source_quote: You will not receive overtures of peace or submission from Indians, but will attack and kill every male Indian over twelve years of age.
notes: Order confirmed verbatim. Superiors countermanding it (Pope) and the Tongue River attack on Black Bear's Arapaho camp (Aug. 29, 1865) and Pawnee scouts killing 24 Cheyenne were not checked here.

That only these four were Council of 44 chiefs and that most Northern people rejected the treaty because the Council did not approve it is TREC's account, not shown in the record.
corrected_instrument_cite: Treaty of May 10, 1868, 15 Stat. 655; Kappler II 1012
notes: No Royce area in the atlas is tied to this treaty; the ICC tied it to the Northern half-interest in the 1851 lands (Royce 426). The signature list mixes Cheyenne and Arapaho without labels.

source_title: Peter J. Powell, as quoted by TREC p. 290; Treaty of May 10, 1868, Art. 2
source_quote: do  hereby  relinquish,  release,  and  surrender  to  the  United States,  all  right,  claim,  and  interest  in  and  to  all  territory  outside  the two  reservations  above  mentioned
notes: The oral promise (via Powell) cannot be checked against the written text, which offers only the Southern reservation or the Sioux reservation. The gap between spoken promise and written text is the point TREC makes; attribute to Powell. Treaty council transcript (Peace Commission proceedings, NARA RG 48/75) would settle.

source_title: Treaty of May 10, 1868, Art. 2
source_quote: except  the  right  to  roam  and  hunt  while  game  shall  be  found  in  sufficient  quantities  to  justify  the  chase
corrected_summary: Article 2 had the Northern Cheyenne and Arapaho accept a home on the Southern Cheyenne-Arapaho reservation or the Sioux reservation and relinquish all territory outside them, keeping a right to roam and hunt while game lasted. The relinquishment is not written as conditional on settling there. TREC's conclusion that the treaty is void because the placements failed is its own legal argument. The Northern Cheyenne reservation was later set by executive order (1884).
notes: Some Northern Arapaho did go to Wind River and some Northern Cheyenne to Indian Territory (1877) and Red Cloud agency, so "never happened" is overstated.

source_title: Agreement of Sept. 1876, ratified by Act of Feb. 28, 1877; Treaty of May 10, 1868, Art. 8; United States v. Sioux Nation (1980)
source_quote: executed by the above Ogallalla Sioux, Chey- ennes, and Arapahoes, at Red Cloud agency, on the 20th day of Sep- tember, A. D. 1876
corrected_summary: Five Northern Cheyenne (Living Bear, Spotted Elk, Black Bear, Turkey Legs, Calfskin Shirt) and six Northern Arapaho signed the agreement at Red Cloud agency on Sept. 20, 1876; Congress ratified it Feb. 28, 1877, before the Northern Cheyenne were removed south in 1877. So TREC's claim that Cheyenne already removed to Oklahoma could not have signed is contradicted. The majority-consent objection stands: the 1868 Northern treaty (Art. 8) required a majority of adult males for any cession of its reservations, and the Supreme Court noted the 1876 agreement was signed by only about 10 percent of adult male Sioux.
notes: Art. 8 of the 1868 Northern treaty applies to cession of "the reservations herein described", so its reach to the 1876 cession is TREC's argument. The Sioux Nation 10 percent figure concerns the 1868 Sioux treaty's three-fourths rule (Art. 12), not the Cheyenne.

source_title: Agreement of 1876, ratified Feb. 28, 1877, Arts. 1-5
source_quote: relinquish and cede to the United States all the territory lying outside
notes: Art. 1 ends "including all privileges of hunting; and article 16 of said treaty is hereby abrogated." A.G. Boone is among the commissioners named in the ratifying act. Arts. 4-5 not re-read line by line.
